Juvenile sandfish (Holothuria scabra) emerge from the planktonic larval phase at a body length of approximately 1 cm  immediately following settlement and metamorphosis. This post-metamorphic length represents a critical size threshold, below which the bipinnaria and auricularia larvae filter-feed on phytoplankton and are highly vulnerable to predation. At 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the time since birth required to achieve this metamorphic milestone is roughly 15 days , a value that aligns well with developmental rates recorded for related aspidochirote holothurians such as Holothuria atra. The newly settled individual attaches to seagrass rhizomes and fine sandy substrata, where it begins active deposit feeding, grazing on surface diatoms and organic detritus. Its initial wet weight at birth has been estimated at 0.0000042 grams [Wwb = 0.0000042 grams], a value derived from the mean egg diameter of 200 µm and consistent with the small yolk reserves typical of planktotrophic echinoderm larvae. This minuscule hatchling mass has profound consequences for early survival, as the post-larval bout of exogenous feeding onset must coincide directly with adequate seston concentrations in the shallow nursery habitats.

Following the larval-juvenile transition, the post-metamorphic juvenile enters a prolonged phase of allometric growth and gonad maturation. Field surveys and aquaculture growth experiments conducted at a stable rearing temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C] indicate that puberty, defined by the first detectable signs of gametogenesis onset, occurs at approximately 365 days after birth [tp = approximately 365 days after birth]. At this developmental stage, the individual attains a length at puberty of 17.9 cm [Lp = 17.9 cm], which corresponds to a wet weight at puberty of roughly 180 grams [Wwp = roughly 180 grams]. The timing of sexual maturation is notably delayed relative to some other commercially exploited sea cucumbers, such as Apostichopus japonicus, which may mature within one year under optimal thermal regimes. This slower tempo likely reflects the trade-off between rapid somatic growth and the energetic costs of maintaining the spacious body cavity and robust body wall that sandfish use for burrowing and predator evasion. Throughout this subadult phase, individuals forage actively on intertidal sediment flats, ingesting large volumes of carbonate sand and assimilating organic carbon from bacterial biofilms.

Sandfish attain their maximum adult body dimensions only after several additional years of continuous feeding and growth. The ultimate length of this species has been documented at 40 cm [Li = 40 cm], with a corresponding ultimate wet weight of 2000 grams [Wwi = 2000 grams], based on large specimens collected from pristine seagrass meadows in the Western Pacific. At a constant ambient temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the lifespan of Holothuria scabra reaches approximately 14,600 days [am = approximately 14,600 days], which equates to roughly 40 years in absolute terms. This extreme longevity places the sandfish among the longest-lived of tropical holothurians, surpassing the typical maxima of 10 to 15 years reported for many temperate aspidochirotid species. The ability to reach such an advanced age is facilitated by a low natural mortality rate in adults, likely attributable to the chemical defenses (holothurins) present in their body wall and the lack of a conspicuous skeletal structure. These same traits, however, render the species highly susceptible to overfishing, as recruitment failure can go undetected for decades due to the continued presence of large old individuals.

Reproductive effort in sexually mature sandfish is substantial, reflecting the species' strategy as a broadcast spawner in shallow coastal waters. At 25 °C [T = 25 °C], gravid females exhibit a maximum reproductive output equivalent to approximately 46,575 eggs per day, though this value represents only a theoretical upper bound observed during synchronized spawning events in aquaculture ponds. Under natural conditions, this daily rate translates into two readily measured sub-expressions: a clutch size of roughly 17 million eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = roughly 17 million eggs per spawning event], coupled with a spawning frequency of approximately one event per year [F_R_i = approximately one event per year]. The trade-off between the extremely high fecundity per event and the relatively low reproductive frequency is characteristic of echinoderms that inhabit unpredictable, nutrient-poor environments, where the tactical release of vast gamete clouds maximizes the probability of external fertilization despite low population densities. Spawning itself is often cued by environmental pheromones, lunar cycles, and a sharp rise in temperature, ensuring that gamete release is synchronous across the local population.

Age at birth for sandfish is negligible from a demographic perspective, as the fertilised ovum hatches into a planktotrophic larva within 1 day [ab = 1 day] at 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. Early-stage incubation studies at 25 °C [T = 25 °C] confirmed that embryonic development proceeds rapidly under warm tropical conditions. This extraordinarily short incubation period is typical of small-yolked echinoderm eggs, where the transition from the cleavage-stage embryo to the free-swimming blastula-stage embryo occurs within hours of syngamy. The subsequent metamorphic competence of the larva is reached at 15 days since birth , as previously noted, after which the bilateral larva undergoes a dramatic body plan reorganisation involving arm resorption, substratum attachment, and the development of the adult rudiment at a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. The synchrony among these early life-history transitions is critical for successful recruitment; any mismatch between the timing of metamorphic competence and the availability of suitable nursery habitats leads to complete cohort failure. These demographic bottlenecks create a life-history profile that is highly sensitive to both natural environmental variability and anthropogenic disturbance.
